rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: They say Egypt had four gates, and the brothers entered through all four as Jacob directed.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون (¬3): كان لمصر أربعة أبواب فدخلوها من أبوابها كلها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Separate entry could not repel a decree or event God had ordained.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬4): يريد ما كان ذلك ليرد قضاء قضاه الله ولا أمرا قدره الله

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: If the evil eye was decreed, it would strike them whether they entered together or apart.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق (¬5) فتأويل {ما كان يغني عنهم من الله من شيء} أن العين # لو قدر أن تصيبهم

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: God had not decreed that the evil eye would destroy them together, so separation made no difference.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأنباري: معناه لم يسبق في علم الله أن العين تهلكهم عند الاجتماع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the first parsing, min introduces the object and an omitted “if He decreed” is understood; the verse confirms Jacob’s statement.
rows.anchor: وعلى ما ذكر من التأويل يكون التقدير: ما كان يغني عنهم ذلك الدخول من الأبواب المتفرقة

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Alternatively nothing could protect them from God even alongside His decree; min is a subject marker and “with His decree” is omitted.
rows.anchor: وذكر أبو إسحاق (¬1) وجها آخر فقال: وجائز أن يكون لا يغني عنهم مع قضاء الله شيء

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: The exception is separate from the preceding category: Jacob’s wish was fulfilled by separate entry, out of care and fear of the evil eye.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج (¬3): "حاجة" استثناء ليس من الأول. المعنى: لكن حاجة في نفس يعقوب قضاها

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: They explain the need as an inward pang and preoccupation relieved by the brothers’ separate entry.
rows.anchor: والمفسرون (¬4) فسروا الحاجة هاهنا الحزازة والهمة.

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: A need may be called a heart-pang because it affects the heart and burdens the self; removing it is called fulfilling it.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري: وقد يقال للحاجة: حزازة لأنها تؤثر في القلب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He understands Jacob to possess certainty and knowledge of God.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬1): لذو يقين ومعرفة بالله.

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: He glosses knowledge as action; Saʿid’s report from Qatada likewise calls Jacob one who acts on what he knows.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي (¬2): لذو عمل، ونحو هذا روى سعيد عن قتادة

rows.speaker: سعيد عن قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada’s report says Jacob acts on what he knows.
rows.anchor: روى سعيد عن قتادة (¬3): قال: إنه لعامل بما علم.

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: A person who does not act cannot be called knowledgeable.
rows.anchor: قال سفيان (¬4): من لا يعمل لا يكون عالما

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: He accepts al-Kalbi’s reading linguistically: knowledge can name action because it begins, produces, and underlies it, as Jesus is called God’s word because he came to be by the word.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري (¬5): والذي قاله الكلبي جائز تحتمله اللغة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: On one parsing, ma is a verbal noun and its pronoun refers to Jacob: he has knowledge because God taught him; the lām is causal, as in 100:8.
rows.anchor: وهذا معنى قول قتادة (¬6). ويمكن أن تكون "ما"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, ma means “that which,” with its pronoun referring back to it: Jacob has knowledge because of what God taught and made clear to him.
rows.anchor: ويمكن أن تكون "ما" بمعنى "الذي" والهاء عائدة عليها، ويكون التأويل

rows.speaker: التفسير
rows.claim: Another gloss is that Jacob understands, retains, and attends to what God taught him.
rows.anchor: وقيل في التفسير: وإنه لذو فهم لما علمناه أي ذو حفظ

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The praise recognizes Jacob’s knowledge that caution cannot avert destiny and what is decreed will occur.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل المعاني: مدحه الله تعالى بالعلم لقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Most people do not know” may mean they do not know Jacob’s knowledge, or do not know that he possesses this quality.
rows.anchor: ذكر في هذا قولين: أحدهما (¬1): ولكن أكثر الناس لا يعلمون علم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He identifies them as unbelievers, ignorant of what God inspires in His friends.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في قوله (¬4): {ولكن أكثر الناس لا يعلمون} يريد المشركين

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
rows.claim: The brothers brought Benjamin; Joseph praised their compliance, arranged generous hospitality, and lodged them two to a room.
rows.anchor: قال محمد بن إسحاق (¬5) وغيره من المفسرين (¬6): إن إخوة يوسف لما أقدموا أخاه عليه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Joseph brought Benjamin to stay with him because he was alone, so that he would feel at ease rather than lonely and frightened; Hasan and Qatada gloss awā as embracing and lodging him.
rows.anchor: فذلك قوله: {آوى إليه أخاه} أي ضمه إليه وأنزله معه. قاله الحسن (¬7) وقتادة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One report says Joseph disclosed his identity as Joseph son of Rachel and told Benjamin to keep it secret from the others.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬9): قال له يوسف: أنا يوسف بن راحيل.

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb and al-Shaʿbi instead say Joseph did not disclose his identity; he comforted Benjamin by saying he would be a brother in place of the lost brother Benjamin described.
rows.anchor: وقال وهب (¬3) والشعبي (¬4): لم يعترف له بالنسبة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Do not grieve or be saddened; Qatada and others give the same gloss.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬5): يريد فلا تغتم ولا تحزن.

rows.speaker: أهل اللغة
rows.claim: Tabtaʾis is a derived form from buʾs, hardship and distress: may hardship not befall you.
rows.anchor: {تبتئس} تفعيل من البؤس وهو الضر والشدة، أي لا يلحقنك بؤس. هذا قول أهل اللغة (¬7).

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The expression means bringing distress upon oneself through grief.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل المعاني (لا تبتئس): اجتلاب البؤس بالحزن.

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: The warning anticipates the brothers’ future theft and accusation; kānū can mean “will,” as Muqatil also explains, and Arabic can use kāna for yakūnu and vice versa when sense is clear.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري (¬8): ندبه إلى أن لا يحزن على ما يقع به من إخوته في المستقبل

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet’s line illustrates past kāna used with future meaning.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر (¬2): فأدركت من قد كان قبلي ولم أدع

rows.speaker: زياد
rows.claim: Ziyad’s verse uses yakūnu where the intended sense is “was,” illustrating the reverse tense substitution.
rows.anchor: وقال زياد (¬3): وانضح جوانب قبره بدمائها

rows.speaker: الكلبي عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report says the brothers taunted Joseph and Benjamin for their maternal grandfather’s idol worship and claimed Rachel had told Joseph to steal her father’s chest of idols so he would stop worshipping them.
rows.anchor: وروى الكلبي عن ابن عباس (¬4): أن إخوة يوسف كانوا يعيرون يوسف وأخاه

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others take the taunt to concern the brothers’ jealousy and efforts to divert their father’s affection; Joseph hopes they will reunite with Jacob too.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون (¬1): {بما كانوا يعملون} من إقامتهم على حسدنا

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: The siqāya was the ṣuwāʿ from which the king drank.
rows.anchor: قال الليث (¬3): السقاية: الصواع الذي كان يشرب فيها الملك.

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another gloss calls it a vessel used for giving drink, here the king’s drinking cup.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: السقاية (¬4): الإناء الذي يسقى فيه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In ʿAṭāʾ’s narration, it was a beryl goblet for water kept before Joseph.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬5) في رواية عطاء: وكان قدحا من زبرجد

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: He says it was a gold cup.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد (¬6): كان كأسا من ذهب.

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq and ʿIkrima say it was a silver drinking vessel set with gems.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن إسحاق (¬7) وعكرمة (¬8): كانت مشربة من فضة مرصعة بالجوهر.

rows.speaker: المفسرون وأهل اللغة
rows.claim: They gloss adh-dhana muʾadhdhin as a caller calling out and an announcer informing people.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون وأهل اللغة (¬1): نادى مناد وأعلم معلم.

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Adhdhana can denote repeated notification because the verb pattern faʿʿala implies repetition, though it may be one notification if faʿʿala means afʿala.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري (¬2): (أذن) معناه أعلم إعلاما بعد إعلام

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: He sees no difference between adhintu and ādhantu in the sense “I informed”; taʾdhīn is a loud call of notification.
rows.anchor: وقال سيبويه (¬3): الفرق بين أذنت وآذنت، معناه أعلمت، لا فرق بينهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same word is discussed at the cited passages about declaring war and the proclamation of God.
rows.anchor: ومضى الكلام في هذا الحرف مستقصى في مواضع منها قوله: {فأذنوا بحرب من الله}

rows.speaker: أبو الهيثم
rows.claim: ʿĪr covers camels, donkeys, and mules used to transport provisions; restricting it to camels is wrong. Naṣīr says camels are called ʿīr only when used for provisioning.
rows.anchor: قال أبو الهيثم (¬5): كل ما امتير عليه من الإبل والحمير والبغال فهي عير.

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda defines ʿīr as riding camels that carry loads.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة (¬8): العير الإبل الرحولة المركوبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sounder meaning is a loaded caravan; the term originally denoted donkeys and expanded by analogy to every loaded caravan.
rows.anchor: والصحيح في العير أنها القافلة التي فيها الأحمال، والأصل للحمير

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: He says the caravan consisted of donkeys.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد (¬1): كانت العير حميرا.

rows.speaker: مقاتل بن سليمان
rows.claim: He glosses ʿīr as the traveling party.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل (¬2) بن سليمان: العير الرفقة.

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: The word only means a traveling party by standing in for and performing the role of that party.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري: ولا تكون العير رفقة أبدا إلا على قيام مقام الرفقة

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: The address means “people of the caravan”; a group may be addressed as the caravan, as a village or cavalry may stand for its people.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق (¬4): معناه يا أصحاب العير، ولكن قال: (أيتها العير)

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: He supplies an implicit fa-qāla before the herald’s words.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: التقدير فقال: إنكم لسارقون.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Although the brothers had stolen nothing then, the accusation can mean they had stolen Joseph from his father by throwing him in the well.
rows.anchor: قيل (¬5) معناه: إنكم لسارقون يوسف من أبيه، حين طرحتموه في الجب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the caller thought they stole the vessel and did not know Joseph had ordered it placed in Benjamin’s pack by God’s direction; the accusation was not Joseph’s order or knowledge, so the prophet was not lying.
rows.anchor: وقيل (¬6): إن المنادي نادى وعنده أنهم قد سرقوا السقاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The speakers are Joseph’s brothers, the caravan’s owners.
rows.anchor: هو يعني أصحاب العير وهم إخوة يوسف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He reads the brothers as approaching Joseph’s servants, the caller’s party.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬1): يريد أقبل هذه الرفقة على غلمان يوسف.

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: One construction has the brothers approach the caller and supporters; another has the caller and party approach the brothers, since either group can be the antecedent of “approached.”
rows.anchor: قاله أبو بكر (¬2) قال: ويجوز أن يكون المعنى: قال إخوة يوسف وقد أقبل المنادي

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: The ṣuwāʿ is the same measure as ṣāʿ; both it and siqāya are masculine or feminine. Abu Hurayra’s ṣāʿ reading supports their equivalence, and the plurals vary by gender.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق (¬3): الصواع هو الصاع بعينه، وهو يذكر ويؤنث

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says ṣuwāʿ and siqāya name one thing; ṣāʿ also has the plural ṣiyʿān.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن (¬7): الصواع والسقاية شيء واحد

rows.speaker: بعض أهل التأويل
rows.claim: Some distinguish the vessel’s specific name, ṣuwāʿ, from siqāya, a shared descriptive term, like cup, container, and waterskin.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض أهل التأويل (¬1): الاسم الحقيقي لهذا الإناء: الصواع، والسقاية وصف

rows.speaker: جماعة من المفسرين
rows.claim: They describe a measuring vessel shaped like a mukūk or qafīz, used to drink, water animals, and measure grain.
rows.anchor: وقال جماعة من المفسرين: الصواع كان على [صيغة المكوك أو القفيز يشربون فيه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: The guarantor was the caller who made the announcement; zaʿīm means guarantor.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد (¬3): الزعيم: هو المؤذن الذي أذن، وتفسير زعيم كفيل.

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: He says zaʿīm means guarantor in the language of Yemen, as exegetes and linguists generally do.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: الزعيم: الكفيل بلسان أهل اليمن.

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة عن الكسائي
rows.claim: Zaʿamtu bihi means “I guaranteed it”; the verse indicates surety was valid in their law, and the Prophet ruled “the guarantor is liable.”
rows.anchor: أبو عبيدة (¬5) عن الكسائي: زعمت به أزعم زعما وزعامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the amount might seem uncertain, a camel-load of food was known to them, so the guarantee was determinate.
rows.anchor: قلنا: حمل (¬2) بعير من الطعام كان معلوما عندهم فصحت الكفالة به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is surety for property to return a theft before liability arose, though thieves may not lawfully take a reward; perhaps their law permitted it.
rows.anchor: غير أن هذا كفالة مال لرد سرقة، وهو كفالة ما لم يجب

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Arabs swear “ta-Allah” but not “ta-the Merciful”; because Allah is the most frequent oath, they treated wāw as part of its name and replaced it with tāʾ.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء (¬3): العرب لا تقول: تالرحمن، ولا يجعلون مكان الواو تاء إلا في الله

rows.speaker: البصريون
rows.claim: The Basrans regard wāw in wallāh as substituted for tāʾ and vice versa; tāʾ became restricted to this especially apt oath-name because it is a close substitute letter.
rows.anchor: وقال البصريون (¬4): الواو في (والله) بدل من التاء، والتاء بدل من الواو

rows.speaker: المفسرون وجميع أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The brothers swore they did not wrong others or take their property; they reportedly muzzled their camels to keep them from damaging crops, demonstrating no intent to corrupt.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون وجميع أهل المعاني (¬5): حلفوا على علمهم بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They argue they could not be thieves because when they found their own goods among the baggage, they promptly returned them; a thief would not return what he found.
rows.anchor: حين أصبناها مع أمتعتنا، ومن رد ما وجده كيف يكون سارقا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They ask what penalty theft carries if the brothers’ denial is false; the prior exchange already implies the theft under discussion.
rows.anchor: أي ما جزاء السرق إن كنتم كاذبين في قولكم:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Their law enslaved a thief for his theft, functioning like amputation in the later law; the person found with the theft in his pack receives that penalty.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬4) والمفسرون (¬5): كانوا في ذلك الزمان يستعبدون كل سارق بسرقته

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: He parses “its penalty” as the topic and “whoever is found in his bag” as its predicate, with “that is its penalty” added for clarification.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق (¬1): جزاؤه ابتداء، و (من وجد في رحله) الخبر

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: He also allows the whole relative clause as predicate, with the following “his penalty” returning to the topic; repetition makes the referent explicit and avoids ambiguity.
rows.anchor: قال: ويجوز أن يكون قوله: {من وجد في رحله فهو جزاؤه} جملة في موضع خبر الابتداء

rows.speaker: النحويون
rows.claim: The grammarians’ verse repeats “death” instead of a pronoun when emphasizing its severity, illustrating explicit repetition of a referent.
rows.anchor: أنشد النحويون (¬6): لا أرى الموت يسبق الموت شيء

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: His crow verse likewise repeats the noun because of the crow’s ill omen, illustrating emphatic repetition.
rows.anchor: وأنشد ابن الأنباري: ليت الغراب غداة ينعب دائبا

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: “Thus We recompense wrongdoers” means that this is how We recompense them.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق (¬2): أي مثل هذا الجزاء نجزي الظالمين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He specifies the recompense: when a person steals, he is enslaved.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬3): يريد إذا سرق واسترق.

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Since the brothers accepted enslavement as the thief’s penalty, the caller said their belongings must be searched and led them back to Joseph; Joseph searched their bags first to avert suspicion.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: لما قال إخوة يوسف: {ما جئنا لنفسد في الأرض} الآية.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awʿiya is the plural of wiʿāʾ, anything placed in and enclosed by a container.
rows.anchor: والأوعية (¬6) جمع الوعاء وهو كل (ما استودع شيئا) فأحاط به

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: The feminine pronoun may refer to the siqāya, the ṣuwāʿ on a feminine reading, or the theft inferred from context; al-Zajjāj and Ibn al-Anbārī agree.
rows.anchor: قاله الفراء (¬1) والزجاج (¬2) وابن الأنباري

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: The kāf is accusative: the sense is “in this way We devised for Joseph.”
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج (¬4): موضع الكاف نصب، المعنى: مثل ذلك الكيد

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: God inspired Joseph with this stratagem; al-Rabīʿ gives a similar explanation.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس (¬5): يريد ألهمنا يوسف هذا الكيد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He glosses the phrase as God’s making a plan for Joseph.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة (¬7): صنعنا ليوسف.

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: He says God planned for Joseph against his brothers and reunited him with Benjamin.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن إسحاق (¬8): كذلك كدنا له إخوته حتى ضممنا أخاه إليه.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: He says God made a plan for Joseph until Joseph did what he did with his brother.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد (¬9): كاد (¬10) الله له حتى فعل بأخيه ما فعل.

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي عن ثعلب
rows.claim: He defines k-y-d as devising by either wrongful or rightful means; here God inspired the plan to hide the vessel in Benjamin’s pack and detain him.
rows.anchor: وروى ثعلب عن ابن الأعرابي (¬11): الكيد التدبير بباطل أو حق

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Applied to God, k-y-d loses humanly blameworthy connotations: God brings the intended outcome against an unaware, powerless target. His plan encompasses Joseph’s rise contrary to his brothers’ designs, whereas exegetes restrict this verse to the inspired detention stratagem.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو بكر (¬1): {كدنا} وقع خبرا عن الله تعالى، على خلاف معناه في أوصاف المخلوقين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In ʿAṭāʾ’s narration, dīn means the king’s judgment; Qatada also reports “his authority,” which Ibn Qutayba chooses.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬3) في رواية عطاء: في حكم الملك وقضائه.

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Dīn means sovereignty in Arabic, as the cited line of Zuhayr illustrates.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر: والدين معناه في اللغة: السلطان.

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj glosses dīn as the king’s manner or rule; another authority says it is his custom, supported by a cited poem.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج (¬4): في سيرة الملك، وقال غيره (¬5): في عادة الملك.

rows.speaker: أهل التفسير
rows.claim: The king punished theft by flogging and charging double, so Joseph could not detain Benjamin under that law; God enabled it by the brothers’ own declaration that a thief should be enslaved.
rows.anchor: قال أهل التفسير (¬1): كان حكم الملك في السارق أن يضرب ويغرم ضعفي ما سرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Except that God wills” means God willed and inspired this means of keeping Benjamin.
rows.anchor: وهو معنى قوله: {إلا أن يشاء الله} فكان ذلك بمشيئة الله.

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: The particle an is accusative because the omitted preposition bi leaves the verb governing it: Joseph could take him only by God’s will.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق (¬2): موضع "أن" نصب، لما سقط الباء أفضى الفعل

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Joseph could not take his brother and secure him without God’s will, which brought him near and eased what could not otherwise be reached.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو بكر: تأويله: ما كان ليأخذ أخاه في دين الملك ويستوجب ضمه إلا بمشيئة الله

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan explains the exception as God commanding Joseph to do it; exegetes generally call it inspiration.
rows.anchor: وروي عن الحسن (¬3) في قوله: {إلا أن يشاء الله} أي أنه الآمر له بذلك

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: God raises people by showing them sound paths to attain aims; the verse hints at Joseph’s elevation.
rows.anchor: قال أهل المعاني أي (¬4) بما نريه من وجوه الصواب في بلوغ المراد

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: God raises people through gifts, honors, and kinds of knowledge, as He raised Joseph above his brothers.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو بكر (¬5): نرفع درجات من نشاء، بضروب عطايانا وكراماتنا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One interpretation of the knower above every learned person is God, who is beyond need of instruction; Hasan and Saʿīd b. Jubayr hold it too.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول ابن عباس (¬1) والحسن (¬2) وسعيد بن جبير (¬3).

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās rebuked someone for using the wording as a generic maxim, saying God is the Knower above all.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: بئسما قلت: الله هو العلم وهو فوق كل شيء (¬4).

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The majority reading is that among those God raises, one learned person surpasses another until knowledge reaches God; it hints Joseph understood more subtly than his brothers.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول ابن عباس (¬5) في رواية عكرمة. قال: يكون هذا أعلم من هذا

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: A scholar should distrust his own completeness and remain humble before God, since every learned person may be surpassed.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر: قال جماعة من أهل التفسير: إن العالم واجب عليه أن يتهم نفسه

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: When the cup was found in Benjamin’s pack, the brothers accused Rachel of bearing two thieves; Benjamin denied stealing and said he did not know who put it in his baggage. Another report has him suggest that whoever returned their goods placed the cup too.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي وغيره من المفسرين (1): لما خرج الصواع من رحل أخي يوسف

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes differ over whether Joseph had told Benjamin about the plan to detain him.
rows.anchor: والمفسرون مختلفون في أن يوسف هل كان أخبر أخاه بالكيد

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: They call Joseph a thief because he secretly took food from his father’s table during famine and gave it in charity; Wahb gives a similar account.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس (2): يريدون يوسف، وكان يأخذ الطعام من مائدة أبيه سرا

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd b. Jubayr and Qatada say Joseph stole his maternal grandfather’s idol, broke it, and left it on the road.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير (5) وقتادة (6) سرق صنما كان لجده أبي أمه

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq and Mujāhid say Joseph’s grandmother hid Isaac’s inherited belt in his clothes to keep him with her by making him appear a thief.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن إسحاق (¬1) ومجاهد (¬2): إن جدته خبأت في ثيابه منطقة

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: These accounts do not make Joseph a real thief: his brothers figuratively accused him of acts resembling theft, like the report that Abraham told three lies—words that appear false but prove true on examination.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري (¬3): وهو في هذه (كلها غير سارق في الحقيقة لكنه أتى) (¬4) ما يشبه السرق

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Asarra al-kalima means to conceal a word inwardly and not reveal it.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء (¬7): أسر الكلمة أي: أضمرها في نفسه ولم يظهرها.

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: He identifies the concealed word as “you are worse in station,” supplying an elided “reply”: Joseph kept their answer to himself.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري (¬8): والكلمة التي أسرها في نفسه: أنتم شر مكانا

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: He treats the pronoun in “he concealed it” as awaiting explanation by the later clause “you are worse in station.”
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق (¬1): الكناية في "فأسرها" إضمار على شريطة التفسير

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu ʿAlī distinguishes a word explained by a word and a sentence pronoun explained by a sentence inside that clause; examples include niʿma rajulan Zayd and rabbahu rajulan.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي (¬4) فيما استدرك عليه: اعلم أن الإضمار على شريطة التفسير

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: He rejects al-Zajjāj’s analysis because the alleged explanation is separated from the clause containing the pronoun; conditioned explanation pairs a whole sentence or word with the same kind of unit.
rows.anchor: فالذي ذكره أبو إسحاق (¬4) في الآية: أنه إضمار على [شريطة التفسير] (¬5)، لا يستقيم

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Instead, the pronoun may stand for Joseph’s unspoken answer, withheld until later, or for the brothers’ utterance as content rather than sound, kept inwardly for reproach or repayment.
rows.anchor: فإن قلت: فعلام يحمل هذا الضمير في أسرها؟ قلنا يحتمل أن يكون إضمارا للإجابة

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: “You are worse” means worse in deed: they threw Joseph into a well, lied that a wolf killed him, and sold him for twenty dirhams; this is implied rather than necessarily spoken in full.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس (¬4): يريد:

rows.speaker: الضحاك عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: He glosses it as worse in conduct because they wronged their brother and disobeyed their father.
rows.anchor: وروى الضحاك عنه (¬3) في قوله (أنتم شر مكانا) قال: شر صنيعا

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: They are worse in God’s sight than the person they accused, because they stole their brother from their father.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل المعاني (¬4): أنتم شر منزلا عند الله ممن رميتموه بالسرقة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One report says Joseph’s taking food was to please God; Hasan and Qatada say God knows the accusation is false, while al-Zajjāj leaves open whether the brother stole.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء (¬5): أراد أن سرقة يوسف كانت لله رضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The father is “great” either in age or in rank.
rows.anchor: أي في السنن ويجوز أن يكون بمعنى: كبير القدر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Hasan offer that one of the brothers be enslaved in Benjamin’s place.
rows.anchor: قال # ابن عباس (1) والحسن (2): خذ واحدا منا تستعبده بدله.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: They praise Joseph as a benefactor if he lets Benjamin return and accepts one of them instead; Abu Bakr summarizes it as beneficence to them.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (3) وابن إسحاق (4): إنك إذا فعلت ذلك فقد أحسنت إلينا

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Another reading asks Joseph to continue his prior kindness in supplying food and returning their goods; Abu Bakr glosses it as generosity in food and price.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق (5): طالبوه بأن يحسن؛ لأنه كان أعطاهم الطعام ورد إليهم بضاعتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maʿādh Allāh expresses seeking God’s protection; al-Zajjāj parses it as a verbal noun: “I seek refuge in God.”
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج (6): المعنى أعوذ بالله معاذا

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: In “to take only the one with our property,” an means taking no innocent person for a guilty one; it is accusative because min is omitted.
rows.anchor: قاله: أبو إسحاق (8). وقوله تعالى: {إنا إذا لظالمون}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Joseph would be transgressing and unjust if he enslaved anyone other than the one who stole.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد لقد تعديت وظلمت إن استعبدت غير الذي سرقني.

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: A reading attributed to Ibn Kathīr has istaʾyasū and another cited passage has istaʾyas without hamza; the form is equivalent to yaʾisa.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن كثير: استايسوا (¬1)، و (حتى إذا استايس (¬2) الرسل) بغير همز (¬3)

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: He explains metathesis of the root’s middle and first letters and subsequent hamza easing; he rejects lā yaʾs as the verbal noun of āsa, deriving iyās instead from the verb for giving.
rows.anchor: هذا قول أبي علي الفارسي (¬1). وقال غيره:

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another grammarian treats āyis as a dialect form of yāʾis, and āyastu-hu as “I made him despair.”
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: آيس لغة في: يئس وآيسته، أي: أيأسته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The brothers despaired that Joseph would let Benjamin go with them.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬2): يريد يئسوا أن يخلى سبيله معهم.

rows.speaker: أهل اللغة
rows.claim: Khalasa means to become free of admixture; here the brothers were alone without outsiders. Najiy is an active adjective meaning a secret interlocutor, usable for any number or gender like ṣadīq; najwa may also be a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: يقال: خلص الشيء خلوصا، إذا ذهب عنه الشائب من غيره، ومعنى خلصوا هاهنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited Qurʾānic uses apply najiy to one person, najwa to a group, and najwa as the verbal noun for secret counsel.
rows.anchor: قال الله تعالى: {وقربناه نجيا} [مريم: 52] فوصف به الواحد

rows.speaker: الصلتان العبدي
rows.claim: His verse uses najwa as a verbal noun and najiy as the person confided in, warning against revealing secrets.
rows.anchor: والبيت للصلتان العبدي (¬1)، والنجوى فيه مصدر، والنجي صفة

rows.speaker: لبيد
rows.claim: Labīd’s verse attests the plural anjiya for people conferring privately.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول لبيد (¬2): وشهدت أنجية الأفاقة عاليا

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: He says the brothers separated from Benjamin to confer about returning to their father without him; Ibn al-Anbārī agrees.
rows.anchor: فقال أبو إسحاق (¬3): انفردوا وليس معهم أخوهم متناجين فيما يعملون

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: He says they withdrew from other people and conferred among themselves.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن قتيبة (¬4): اعتزلوا الناس ليس معهم غيرهم يتناجون

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: He likewise understands that they withdrew from people to confer; this general reading is the apparent meaning, unlike the view specifying separation from Benjamin.
rows.anchor: وقال الأزهري (¬5): تميزوا عن (¬6) # الناس يتناجون فيما أهمهم

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: He identifies the eldest as Judah, a view also given by Wahb, al-Kalbi, and Muqatil: Judah led in sound judgment, not age.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس (¬1): يعني يهوذا وكان أعقلهم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies him as Shimʿūn, greatest in knowledge and reason, not age.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد (¬5): شمعون، وكان أكبرهم في العلم والعقل لا في السن.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada, al-Suddī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and Kaʿb identify him as Reuben, the eldest by age; the author calls this apparent.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة (¬6) والسدي (¬7) والضحاك (¬8) وكعب (¬9): هو روبيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pledge was the promise to protect Benjamin and return him to their father.
rows.anchor: أي في حفظكم الأخ ورده إلى أبيه

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: The ma may be a verbal noun in the nominative, meaning their failure regarding Joseph had occurred and become manifest.
rows.anchor: وذكر الفراء (¬3) والزجاج (¬4) وابن الأنباري في "ما" ثلاثة أوجه

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: A second parsing makes ma accusative, coordinated with the meaning of “did you not know”: and before that, your failure regarding Joseph.
rows.anchor: الثاني: أن يكون "ما" في موضع نصب نسق على المعنى: {ألم تعلموا أن أباكم}

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: A third parsing treats ma as extra with no syntactic position, yielding simply “and before you failed regarding Joseph.”
rows.anchor: الثالث: أن تكون لغوا لا موضع لها من الإعراب

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Baruḥ means moving from one’s place; Ibn ʿAbbās takes “the land” as his current location, while al-Zajjāj specifies Egypt since otherwise everyone is on land.
rows.anchor: يقال: برح الرجل براحا وبروحا، إذا رام من موضعه، ذكره الفراء (¬1)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He will remain until his father sends word allowing him to come home.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬5): حتى يبعث إلى أبى أن آتيه.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: “Or God decides for me” means God decrees some outcome; another view allows a decision to fight the captor or take another action.
rows.anchor: قال: يريد أو يقضي في أمري شيئا، وقال غيره: أو يحكم الله لي لمحاربة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The best of judges” means the most just and excellent of them.
rows.anchor: {وهو خير الحاكمين}: أعدلهم وأفضلهم.

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: The brothers should say Benjamin “stole” in the king’s judgment or as observers saw it, although they do not know this to be true; this established idiom is stronger than the figurative proposal that his act merely resembled theft.
rows.anchor: ذكر ابن الأنباري في هذا وجهين: أحدهما: أن معناه سرق عند الملك

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Most exegetes say the brothers did not know the real circumstances and attributed theft based on appearances, explaining their claim that they witnessed only what they knew.
rows.anchor: وأكثر المفسرين على أنهم ما عرفوا حقيقة الحال فنسبوا إليه السرق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He glosses “what we knew” as what had become apparent.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬1): يريد بما ظهر.

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: They said Benjamin stole because the theft was found in his baggage before their eyes.
rows.anchor: قال ابن إسحاق (¬2): معناه: ما قلنا أنه سرق إلا بما علمنا

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Testimony is a special kind of knowledge: every testimony is knowledge, but not all knowledge is testimony. A court needs “I testify,” not merely “I know”; testimony is focused and established knowledge, expressed here with bi and elsewhere with ʿalā.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي الفارسي (¬3): شهد الذي يراد به علم هو ضرب من العلم مخصوص

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: They could not know what Benjamin did in his private comings and goings: they guarded him while present, but his affairs were hidden when he was away.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬1): لم نعلم ما كان يصنع في ليله ونهاره ومجيئه وذهابه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid, Qatada, and Hasan say they did not foresee Benjamin would steal; they guaranteed only what they could actually safeguard.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد (¬3) وقتادة (¬4) والحسن (¬5): ما كنا نشعر أن ابنك سيسرق

rows.speaker: ابن كيسان
rows.claim: They did not know Jacob would suffer this loss as he suffered over Joseph; had they known, they would not have taken Benjamin.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن كيسان (¬6): لم نعلم أنك تصاب به كما أصبت بيوسف

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Perhaps facts were not as they appeared; ʿIkrima suggests the cup was planted in Benjamin’s pack overnight, and Ibn Isḥāq says someone could have taken it without the brothers knowing.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء فيما رواه عن ابن عباس: {وما كنا للغيب حافظين} أي: لعله قد غاب عنا أمر

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The elder brother instructs the others to return and explain the circumstances to their father.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل المعاني: معنى الآية: أنه يقول لإخوته {ارجعوا إلى أبيكم} واشرحوا له كيف كانت الحال.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: “Ask the village” means ask its people; the omitted “people” is concise idiomatic ellipsis endorsed by most exegetes.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬2): يريد أهل مصر، وهذا قول عامة المفسرين

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Denying this usage in Arabic is unreasonable; its well-known occurrence in scripture needs no further proof.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي (¬4): ودافع جواز هذا في اللغة كدافع الضرورات

rows.speaker: أبو زيد والكوفيون
rows.claim: Their poem about a mount’s bleat omits “of a she-camel”; the intended meaning is a she-camel’s bleat.
rows.anchor: وأنشد أبو زيد والكوفيون (¬5): حسبت بغام راحلتي عناقا

rows.speaker: النحويون
rows.claim: Poets also replace an annexed-to noun with the annexed noun, as in “they carry ʿAbbās b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib,” meaning Ibn ʿAbbās.
rows.anchor: من ذلك أنشده النحويون: يحملن عباس بن عبد المطلب

rows.speaker: شاعر آخر
rows.claim: The cited line means Jarīr b. al-Khuṭafī; these examples support ellipsis or substitution where context prevents ambiguity.
rows.anchor: وقول آخر (¬2): أرى الخطفي بز الفرزدق شعره

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Alternatively, ask the village and caravan literally: walls, camels, buildings, tents, and roofs will answer miraculously, so no ellipsis or figurative speech is needed.
rows.anchor: وذكر أبو بكر (¬4) في هذا وجها آخر وهو: أن يكون المعنى واسأل القرية والعير

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Hasan, and Qatada identify the village as Egypt; al-Kalbi says it was one of Egypt’s villages.
rows.anchor: وابن عباس (¬1) والحسن (¬2) وقتادة (¬3): على أن المراد بالقرية مصر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: “The caravan with which we came” means its people; exegetes say Canaanites accompanied them.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬5): يريد أهل الرفقة التي كنا فيها

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: The detained brother knew their father would suspect them because of what they did to Joseph, so he told them to make this appeal to clear themselves.
rows.anchor: قال ابن إسحاق (¬7): عرف الأخ المحتبس أن إخوته أهل تهمة عند أبيهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Jacob recounts twelve sons leaving and eleven returning, then eleven leaving and ten returning, then ten leaving and nine returning, expressing bewilderment at repeated losses.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في هذه الآية: لما قدموا على أبيهم وأخبروه اشتد حزنه

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The narrative omits that they returned and repeated Judah’s instructions, after which Jacob replied that their selves had made a matter seem good to them.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون (¬1) وأهل المعاني: هاهنا إيجاز وإضمار

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Unlike his earlier accusation, Jacob is not charging them with deception: their insistence on sending Benjamin brought harm instead of the benefit they expected, as God’s decree overtook them.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري (¬2): لم ينسبهم يعقوب في هذا إلى الكذب والاحتيال

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another view says their selves made them imagine Benjamin had stolen when he had not; the numbers refer to Joseph’s loss, Benjamin’s detention, and the eldest brother staying in Egypt.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره (¬3): معنى قوله هاهنا {سولت لكم أنفسكم أمرا} خيلت لكم أنه سرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob hopes God will bring Joseph, Benjamin, and the son who stayed behind together.
rows.anchor: يعني يوسف وبنيامين، والذي قال: فلن أبرح الأرض.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-ʿAlīm knows Jacob’s deep grief, and al-Ḥakīm governs the successive calamities of losing one son after another.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬1): بشدة حزني {الحكيم} فيما حكم علي بهذا الحزن

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another explanation is that God knows whether his sons are truthful and is wise in governing creation.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: {العليم} بصدق ما يقولونه من كذبه، {الحكيم} في تدبيره لخلقه.

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: When Jacob learned Benjamin was detained, his grief reached its limit and rekindled grief for Joseph, since Benjamin had comforted him after Joseph’s loss; tawallā means he turned away.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون (¬2): لما بلغ يعقوب خبر حبس بنيامين، تتام حزنه

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Asaf is grief over what has passed: when an event grieves and overwhelms you, you are sorrowful and afflicted.
rows.anchor: قال الليث (¬4): إذا جاءك أمر فحزنت له ولم تطقه فأنت آسف

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: The original vocative is yā asafī; the possessive yā may become alif for ease.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج (¬5): والأصل يا أسفي، إلا أن ياء الإضافة يجوز أن تبدل ألفا

rows.speaker: متمم بن نويرة
rows.claim: His elegy shows one sorrow reviving another: seeing a grave renews the poet’s grief for his brother Mālik.
rows.anchor: وقد قال متمم بن نويرة (¬7): فقال أتبكى كل قبر رأيته

rows.speaker: عامة أهل العلم
rows.claim: They say Jacob’s grief was not sinful despair: restrained grief earns reward; a report has Gabriel tell Joseph it equaled that of seventy bereaved women and earned the reward of a hundred martyrs.
rows.anchor: عامة أهل العلم (¬2): على أن قول يعقوب عليه السلام: {يا أسفى على يوسف} ليس منه جزعا مذموما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He glosses the cry as “how long my grief for Joseph!”
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬4) في قوله: {يا أسفى}: يا طول حزني على يوسف.

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says eighty years passed from Joseph’s departure until reunion, with Jacob’s eyes never drying, and no one on earth was more honored by God.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن (¬5): كان بين خروج يوسف من حجر يعقوب إلى يوم التقى معه ثمانون عاما

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada glosses asaf as grief and Mujāhid as anguish; Abu Bakr says those who take it as anguish opposed to patience regard this as Jacob’s error, citing a report where God reproaches his complaint and Jacob asks forgiveness.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة (¬1): يا حزني على يوسف، وقال مجاهد (¬2): يا جزعى على يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His eyes changed to white; Muqatil says he could not see for six years until God restored him through Joseph’s shirt.
rows.anchor: أي انقلبت إلى حال البياض، قال مقاتل (¬5): لم يبصر بهما ست سنين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Grief here means weeping: intense crying whitened Jacob’s eyes, and the cause is named for its effect.
rows.anchor: وفسر ابن عباس (¬6) الحزن هاهنا: بالبكاء يريد: أن عيناه ابيضتا

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some distinguish ḥuzn as weeping and ḥazan as the opposite of joy.
rows.anchor: فقال قوم: الحزن: البكاء، والحزن: ضد الفرح.

rows.speaker: أكثر أهل اللغة
rows.claim: Most linguists treat ḥuzn and ḥazan as two dialect forms; Yunus from Abū ʿAmr says the accusative has fatḥa but nominative/genitive ḍamma, with verses illustrating each.
rows.anchor: وهذا مذهب أكثر أهل اللغة (¬1)، وروى يونس عن أبي عمرو (¬2) قال: إذا كان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He notes the phrase “I complain” is in the nominative position of an introductory clause.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى (¬3): {أشكو (¬4) بثي وحزني إلى الله} قال: هو في موضع رفع بالابتداء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kazeem can mean one who suppresses grief and does not reveal or complain of it; Qatada says Jacob held grief in his heart and kept his mouth sealed, as a poem illustrates.
rows.anchor: قال ابن قتيبة (¬5): يدل عليه قول قتادة (¬6) قال: كظيم على الحزن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Alternatively kazeem means one choked from expressing grief, supported by the verse about Jonah being makẓūm; Ibn ʿAbbās calls Jacob distressed and al-Zajjāj sorrowful.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون بمعنى المكظوم، وهو المسدود عليه طريق حزنه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: “One of the perishing” means dead; the brothers say continued grieving will leave Jacob useless through illness or kill him, seeking to restrain him out of concern.
rows.anchor: أي: من الميتين، قاله قتادة (¬6)، ومعنى الآية: أنهم قالوا لأبيهم

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: After the brothers speak harshly, Jacob says he directs his complaint to God, not to them.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون (¬7): لما رأى غلظتهم وعنفهم به

rows.speaker: أهل اللغة
rows.claim: Bath is worry divulged to a companion; its root evokes spreading and dispersing.
rows.anchor: قال أهل اللغة (¬1): البث: الهم الذي تفضي به إلى صاحبك

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda calls bath the most intense grief and ḥuzn the most intense worry; another view contrasts concealed worry with grief too great to hide, illustrated by the poem.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة (¬2): البث: أشد الحزن، والحزن أشد الهم

rows.speaker: الكلبي عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Jacob knew Joseph was alive: the Angel of Death said he had not taken Joseph’s soul among the souls he collected.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي عن ابن عباس (¬4): وذلك أن ملك الموت أتاه فقال له

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report says Jacob knew Joseph’s dream was true and that the family would bow to him.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس (¬5): وأعلم أن رؤيا يوسف صادقة

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: This shows Jacob surpassed the others in interpretation and reached realities beyond their understanding, according to Muqatil.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري: وهذا يدل على أن يعقوب كان يزيد عليهم في علم العبارة

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: He knew of God’s mercy, power, and compassion toward His friends.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء عن ابن عباس (¬2): وأعلم من رحمة الله وقدرته ورأفته

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He knew God’s choice for him justified his good expectation.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة (¬3): أعلم من اختيار الله عز وجل لي

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: After the sons described the king’s conduct, Jacob hoped the king might be Joseph and sent them to search.
rows.anchor: قال السدي (¬4): لما أخبره بنوه بسيرة الملك وقوله

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another report says Jacob saw the Angel of Death in a dream, swore Joseph was not dead, and directed his sons toward Egypt.
rows.anchor: (وقيل: (¬5) إنه رأى ملك الموت في المنام، فأقسم والله ما قبضت روح يوسف) (¬6)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taḥassus means seeking something through the senses.
rows.anchor: والتحسس: تطلب الشيء بالحاسة.

rows.speaker: أبو معاذ
rows.claim: He explains taḥassus as something like listening and looking carefully.
rows.anchor: قال أبو معاذ (¬7): التحسس: شبه التسمع والتبصر.

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Taḥassastu al-khabar means investigating and seeking news to obtain it; aḥassa means to know and find it, and Ibn ʿAbbās says to search for Joseph.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيد (¬1): تحسست الخبر: بحثته وطلبته لأخذه

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Although Arabic ordinarily says taḥassastu ʿan fulān, min here may replace ʿan; alternatively min is partitive, meaning seek some news about Joseph.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر (¬3): يقال: تحسست عن فلان، ولا يقال: من فلان

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Rūḥ is relief from grief of the heart; Abū ʿAmr defines it as deliverance or the soothing breeze a person experiences.
rows.anchor: قال الأصمعي (¬4): الروح الاستراحة من غم القلب، وقال أبو عمرو (¬5): الروح الفرج

rows.speaker: أهل اللغة
rows.claim: They connect r-w-ḥ with movement and vibration: whatever a person takes pleasure in and delights in is rūḥ.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل اللغة (¬6) ما يتركب (¬7) من الراء، والواو والحاء كثير

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In ʿAṭāʾ’s report, rūḥ Allāh means God’s mercy, as Qatada, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and al-Kalbi also say.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء (¬1): {ولا تيأسوا من روح الله} يريد من رحمة الله

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: A report from Qatada through Maʿmar glosses it as God’s bounty.
rows.anchor: وروى معمر عن قتادة (¬5): من فضل الله.

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: He glosses it as relief from God, or the spirit He brings.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد (¬6): من فرج الله، ولا تيأسوا من الروح الذي يأتي به الله.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A believer hopes for good from God during hardship and thanks and praises Him in ease, unlike an unbeliever.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬7): يريد أن المؤمن من الله على خير يرجوه في الشدائد

rows.speaker: أهل اللغة
rows.claim: The narrative elides that they returned to Egypt before entering Joseph’s presence; al-ḍurr is hunger and need affecting them and their dependents.
rows.anchor: قال أهل اللغة (¬8): التأويل في الكلام متروك يستدل عليه، والتقدير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zajja means to drive or push little by little, as clouds move, a cow drives its calf, and one fends someone off with words; eking out a living means getting by on little.
rows.anchor: معني الإزجاء في اللغة (¬1): السوق (¬2) والدفع قليلا قليلا، ومثله: التزجية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In reports through ʿIkrima and Bādhān, the brothers brought debased counterfeit coins that would not buy food.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬1): كانت دراهم رديئة زيوفا لا تنفق في ثمن الطعام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In ʿAṭāʾ’s report, Egyptian coins bore Joseph’s image while theirs did not, making their currency inferior.
rows.anchor: وفسر في رواية عطاء كيف كانت الدراهم فقال (¬2): وذلك أن دراهم مصر كانت

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd b. Jubayr calls the currency low quality; al-Farrāʾ says their goods fetched coins below the price of good ones.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول سعيد بن جبير (¬3): أنها كانت دراهم فسولا، واختيار الفراء (¬4)

rows.speaker: سعيد عن قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada and several other authorities call the consignment small; one report describes a small remainder after the sack and rope.
rows.anchor: وروى سعيد عن قتادة (¬5): {ببضاعة مزجاة} قال يسيرة، وقال عبد الله بن الحارث (¬6): قليلة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The scant goods were variously identified: Ibn ʿAbbās’s report through Ibn Jurayj, likewise through Ibn Abī Mulayka and Ibn Zayd; Hasan says curds, ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Ḥārith clarified butter and wool, Juwaybir from al-Ḍaḥḥāk sandals and leather, and Muqatil b. Ḥayyān and al-Kalbi green seed and al-ḍabūr.
rows.anchor: وذكرنا قول ابن عباس فيها في رواية ابن جريج ومثله روى عنه ابن أبي مليكة (¬6)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Muzjāh derives from eking out a living: the small consignment could sustain them day by day, not provide abundance.
rows.anchor: فقال أبو إسحاق (¬1): من قولهم: فلان يزجي العيش، أي: يدفع بالقليل

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: The coins were muzjāh because they were rejected and passed back; his cited poem describes those circumstances compelling a destitute guest and widow to get by.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيد (¬2): إنما قيل للدراهم الرديئة مزجاة؛ لأنها مردودة مدفوعة

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another explanation is deferred, rejected currency accepted only by someone forced by need and lacking better money.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره (¬4) (بضاعة مزجاة) مؤخرة مدفوعة عن الإنفاق

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi calls muzjāh a foreign, non-Arab word.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي (1): مزجاة لغة العجم.

rows.speaker: الهيثم بن عدي
rows.claim: Al-Haytham b. ʿAdī specifically attributes the word to Coptic.
rows.anchor: قال الهيثم بن عدي (2): هي من لغة القبط.

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: He rejects the Coptic attribution: a word with recognizable Arabic morphology and derivation should not be assigned to Coptic speech, which does not inflect according to Arabic patterns.
rows.anchor: قال الأنباري (3): لا ينبغي أن يجعل حرف عربي معروف المباني والاشتقاق والتصرف
